  8336	
  8337	Definition. `waveGreen d s` is, for `d = 1`, `(1/2)` Lebesgue measure
  8338	restricted to the open ball `|x| < s`; for `d = 2`, Lebesgue measure with
  8339	density `1_{|x|<s} (2 pi sqrt(s^2 - |x|^2))^(-1)` (inside the ball the root
  8340	is of a positive number, so no `sqrt` or division junk value enters); for
  8341	`d = 3`, `(s/(4 pi)) map (w -> s w) volume.toSphere`; for every other `d`,
  8342	the zero measure. For `d = 3` this is a DEFINITIONAL CHOICE (Le's decision 4
  8343	for wave L6): Mathlib's `Measure.toSphere` (which satisfies
  8344	`sigma(A) = 3 vol{r w : 0 < r < 1, w in A}` for measurable `A`, the cone
  8345	measure) is taken as the surface measure of the unit sphere, and
  8346	`sigma_s = s^2 map (w -> s w) sigma_1` as that of the radius-`s` sphere, so
  8347	`sigma_s/(4 pi s) = (s/(4 pi)) map (w -> s w) sigma_1`. Neither
  8348	identification with a Hausdorff or Riemannian surface measure is proved.

  8448

  8450	Archimedes' law for Mathlib's sphere measure, and the extension of the
  8451	Green-smoothing identification of `L:damped-homogeneous-norms` to every
  8452	`d = 1, 2, 3`, in `StratonovichHAMSecondMoment/WaveGreenFourier.lean`.
  8453	Sources (`notes/notes_stratonovich_ham_second_moment.tex` at `a284420`):
  8454	`G_s hat(xi) = sin(s norm(xi))/norm(xi)`, value `s` at `xi = 0` (lines
  8455	777-778, before `E:damped-norm-definitions`); the display
  8456	`G_h hat(xi) = sin(h norm(xi))/norm(xi)`, `G_h(R^d) = h` (lines 4740-4744, in
  8457	the proof of `L:low-alpha-convolution`, lines 4702-4757), which the TeX quotes
  8458	from the source's (2.3)-(2.5), p. 7, without proof; the identity is also used

     3	  226|   Let $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. The spatial covariance is a
     4	  227|   nonnegative, even, positive-definite tempered Radon measure $\Gamma$ on
     5	  228|   $\R^d$, with positive even tempered Radon spectral measure $\mu$ in the
     6	  229|   convention
     7	  230|   \[
     8	  231|     \Gamma=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(\ud\xi)
     9	  232|     \quad\text{in the sense of tempered distributions}.

    11	  234|   The symbol $\gamma$ in~\eqref{E:cov} denotes this covariance as a function

    13	  236|   $c > 0$, $\Gamma(cA) = c^{d-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$, and

    15	  238|     \alpha_0+\alpha<2,

    17	  240|   with $0 < \alpha < d$, or $\alpha = d = 1$. In particular, the last case

    64	  803| \begin{lemma}[Homogeneous damped norms and temporal tails]
    65	  804|   \label{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}
    66	  805|   Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, the integrals
    67	  806|   in~\eqref{E:damped-norm-definitions} are finite for every $\theta > 0$, with
    68	  807|   $N_2(\theta)^2 \ge 0$, and
    69	  808|   \[
    70	  809|     N_0(\theta)=\theta^{-2},\qquad
    71	  810|     N_1(\theta)=\theta^{\alpha+\alpha_0-2}N_1(1),\qquad
    72	  811|     N_2(\theta)^2=\theta^{-\beta}N_2(1)^2,
    73	  812|     \quad\beta=4-\alpha-\alpha_0.
    74	  813|   \]
    75	  814|   Let
    76	  815|   \[
    77	  816|     K_M(r)=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(\alpha_0)}
    78	  817|     \int_M^\infty e^{-\lambda|r|}\lambda^{\alpha_0-1}\ud\lambda.
    79	  818|   \]
    80	  819|   Denote by $N_1^{(M)}(1)$ the first norm with $\lambda > M$, and by
    81	  820|   $N_2^{(M)}(1)$ the second norm with $K_M(s-t)$ in place of
    82	  821|   $|s-t|^{-\alpha_0}$. Then
    83	  822|   \begin{equation}\label{E:damped-tail-norms}
    84	  823|     N_1^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
    85	  824|     N_2^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0\quad(M\to\infty).

   185	 2011|   improves the crude quadratic time scale under homogeneity. It does not itself
   186	 2012|   prove Theorem~\ref{T:intro-upper}; Section~\ref{S:interval-upper} uses a different

   188	 2014|   sufficient to prove Theorem~\ref{T:intro-upper}}: even with exact homogeneous norm scaling, the
   189	 2015|   resulting majorant has exponent $\rho > \kappa$. The order coefficient has
   190	 2016|   factorial denominator $(k!)^{3-\alpha-\alpha_0}$, whereas the desired scale
   191	 2017|   requires $(k!)^{3-\alpha}$; the missing factor is $(k!)^{\alpha_0}$, up to
   192	 2018|   exponential factors in $k$. Counting the $2k+1$ chain-length splits does not
   193	 2019|   cause this loss, since it can be absorbed into an exponential factor. This
   194	 2020|   conclusion does not rule out a more refined application retaining temporal
   195	 2021|   order or grouping pairings before estimating them, and does not disprove the

   214	 2072| \begin{lemma}[Two static contraction bounds]\label{L:phase-contractions}
   215	 2073|   For $\lambda > 0$, $q \in \R^3$, $a > 0$, and $\epsilon > 0$,

216	 2074|   \begin{align}
   217	 2075|     \int_{\R^3}\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{\lambda^2+|q+\xi|^2}
   218	 2076|     &\le R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2},
   219	 2077|     \label{E:phase-resolvent}\\
   220	 2078|     \left|T_\epsilon(a,q)\right|
   221	 2079|     &\le D_\Gamma a^{1-\alpha},
   222	 2080|     \label{E:phase-trace}\\
   223	 2081|     T_\epsilon(a,q)
   224	 2082|     &:=\int_{\R^3}e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)
   225	 2083|     =\int_{\R^3}\widehat{G}_a(q+\xi)e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2}
   226	 2084|     \mu(\ud\xi).\nonumber
   227	 2085|   \end{align}
   228	 2086| \end{lemma}
   229	 2087| 
   230	 2088| \begin{proof}
   231	 2089|   Homogeneity and Fourier uniqueness give $\mu(B_r) = Vr^\alpha$. In particular,
   232	 2090|   there is no origin atom. For $s > 0$, Schwartz Fourier pairing yields
   233	 2091|   \[
   234	 2092|     \int e^{-s|q+\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
   235	 2093|     =\int p_{2s}(x)e^{iq\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x)
   236	 2094|     \le\int p_{2s}(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
   237	 2095|     =\int e^{-s|\xi|^2}\mu(\ud\xi).
   238	 2096|   \]
   239	 2097|   The integrals are finite. Evenness makes the middle integral real, and
   240	 2098|   nonnegativity of $\Gamma$ gives the inequality. Multiply by $e^{-\lambda^2s}$
   241	 2099|   and integrate in $s$. Nonnegative Tonelli on the spectral side gives the
   242	 2100|   resolvent comparison. At $q = 0$ its value is
   243	 2101|   \[
   244	 2102|     \alpha V\int_0^\infty\frac{r^{\alpha-1}}{\lambda^2+r^2}\ud r
   245	 2103|     =R_\alpha\lambda^{\alpha-2}.
   246	 2104|   \]
   247	 2105|   This proves~\eqref{E:phase-resolvent}.
   248	 2106| 
   249	 2107|   Since $\mu$ is tempered, its Gaussian weighting is finite. Fourier Fubini
   250	 2108|   therefore gives the identity for $T_\epsilon$. The measure
   251	 2109|   $\Gamma_\epsilon(x)G_a(\ud x)$ is finite and nonnegative, whence
   252	 2110|   $|T_\epsilon(a,q)| \le T_\epsilon(a,0)$. The radial distribution function of
   253	 2111|   $\Gamma$ is $\Gamma(B_r) = Mr^{3-\alpha}$. Thus, for every nonnegative radial
   254	 2112|   Schwartz function $F$,
   255	 2113|   \[
   256	 2114|     \int F(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
   257	 2115|     =(3-\alpha)M\int_0^\infty F(r)r^{2-\alpha}\ud r
   258	 2116|     =c_\Gamma\int_{\R^3}F(x)|x|^{-\alpha}\ud x.
   259	 2117|   \]
   260	 2118|   Apply this to $F = G_a*p_{2\epsilon}$, which is radial and Schwartz.
   261	 2119|   Nonnegative Fubini gives
   262	 2120|   \[
   263	 2121|     T_\epsilon(a,0)
   264	 2122|     =c_\Gamma[p_{2\epsilon}*(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})](0)
   265	 2123|     \le c_\Gamma\sup_z(G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z).
   266	 2124|   \]
   267	 2125|   Write $r = |z|$. The spherical wave measure has mass $a$, and direct
   268	 2126|   integration over its normal coordinate gives, for $r > 0$,
   269	 2127|   \[
   270	 2128|     (G_a*|\cdot|^{-\alpha})(z)
   271	 2129|     =\frac{(a+r)^{2-\alpha}-|a-r|^{2-\alpha}}
   272	 2130|     {2r(2-\alpha)}.
   273	 2131|   \]
   274	 2132|   For $r < a/2$, distances from $z$ to the sphere are at least $a/2$, giving the
   275	 2133|   bound $2^\alpha a^{1-\alpha}$. For $r > 2a$, they are at least $a$, giving
   276	 2134|   $a^{1-\alpha}$. On $a/2 \le r \le 2a$, the displayed formula is at most
   277	 2135|   $3^{2-\alpha}a^{1-\alpha}/(2-\alpha)$. These bounds also cover the endpoints
   278	 2136|   by continuity and give~\eqref{E:phase-trace}. This proves
   279	 2137|   Lemma~\ref{L:phase-contractions}.
   280	 2138| \end{proof}

   283	 3600| \begin{lemma}[The finite terminal-chain Wick formula]\label{L:terminal-wick}

   285	 3602|   $d = 1,2,3$, with covariance $\mathcal{K}(s,y;r,z)$. Suppose that $V =
   286	 3603|   \sup_{s,y}\E|\mathcal{W}(s,y)|^2 < \infty$, and that the field is jointly
   287	 3604|   continuous in mean square on each open cell of a finite partition of $[0,T]$,
   288	 3605|   times $\R^d$. Define $Y_0 = 1$ and
   289	 3606|   \[
   290	 3607|     Y_n(T,x)=\int\prod_{j=1}^n\mathcal{W}(s_j,y_j)
   291	 3608|     \,\mathsf{g}_n^{T,x}(\ud\boldsymbol s,\ud\boldsymbol y).
   292	 3609|   \]

   294	 3611|   \begin{equation}\label{E:terminal-term-majorant}
   295	 3612|     \|Y_n(T,x)\|_2
   296	 3613|     \le\sqrt{(2n-1)!!}\,V^{n/2}\frac{T^{2n}}{(2n)!},
   297	 3614|     \qquad n\ge1.
   298	 3615|   \end{equation}

   300	 3617|   (s_1,\ldots,s_m,r_1,\ldots,r_n)$ and $\boldsymbol\eta =
   301	 3618|   (y_1,\ldots,y_m,z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. Then

   305	 3622|   \end{equation}

   307	 3624|   \begin{equation}\label{E:terminal-pairing-integral}
   308	 3625|     \begin{split}
   309	 3626|       \mathcal{T}_{m,n,D}^{\mathcal{K}}
   310	 3627|       ={}&\int_{[0,T]^m_<\times[0,T]^n_<}
   311	 3628|       \ud\boldsymbol s\,\ud\boldsymbol r
   312	 3629|       \int_{(\R^d)^m\times(\R^d)^n}\\
   313	 3630|       &\quad\times\prod_{j=1}^m

   320	 3637|   \end{equation}

   323	 3640|   $\mathcal{K} \ge 0$, every integral above is nonnegative. Consequently,
   324	 3641|   entrywise comparison $0 \le \mathcal{K}_1 \le \mathcal{K}_2$ compares all

   552	 5167| \begin{lemma}[Riesz spatial maxima]\label{L:higher-riesz}

   554	 5169|   < 2$, Hypothesis~\ref{H:spatial-maximum} holds with the optimal uniform

   556	 5171|   3/2$, it holds with
   557	 5172|   \[
   558	 5173|     M_2=c\left\{4^\alpha+
   559	 5174|     \frac{2\alpha}{3/2-\alpha}4^{\alpha-3/2}\right\}.
   560	 5175|   \]

   565	 5180|   measures are

   568	 5183|     {2\pi\sqrt{h^2-|y|^2}},\qquad
   569	 5184|     G_h^{(3)}(\ud y)=\frac{\sigma_h(\ud y)}{4\pi h},
   570	 5185|   \]

   572	 5187|   mass $h$ and satisfy $G_h(hA) = hG_1(A)$. Thus, the unsmoothed convolution is
   573	 5188|   $ch^{1-\alpha}F_d(z/h)$, where $F_d(w) = \int G_1^{(d)}(\ud
   574	 5189|   y)|y+w|^{-\alpha}$. In dimension three spherical coordinates give, for $\rho =
   575	 5190|   |w| > 0$,
   576	 5191|   \[
   577	 5192|     F_3(w)=\frac{(1+\rho)^v-|1-\rho|^v}{2v\rho},
   578	 5193|     \qquad v=2-\alpha\in(0,1).
   579	 5194|   \]

   581	 5196|   (1+s)^{v-1}$ on $[-\rho,\rho]$. Its derivative has numerator
   582	 5197|   $\rho[f(\rho)+f(-\rho)]-\int_{-\rho}^\rho f(s)\ud s \ge 0$, by the endpoint
   583	 5198|   chord bound for a convex function. For $\rho > 1$, every distance
   584	 5199|   $\sqrt{1+\rho^2+2\rho u}$, $-1 \le u \le 1$, increases with $\rho$, so its
   585	 5200|   negative power decreases. The formula is continuous at $\rho = 1$ and at zero.

   639	  115|   and compact support forces $g=0$, contrary to $\|g\|_2=1$. Put $Q=g^2$ and
   640	  116|   use the unnormalized Fourier transform

   727	   66|   operator properties and $J_E(f,g) = (\Lambda^{-1}g,-\Lambda f)$. The two

   763	  102| 
   764	  103|   We prove the required compact-perturbation bound for this whole-space phase.
   765	  104|   Translations $\tau_y$ on both entries are isometries on $E$ and commute with
   766	  105|   $S_E(h)$. For fixed $z,w \in E$, their translated pairing is the Fourier
   767	  106|   transform of an $L^1$ function: the two weighted Fourier products are
   768	  107|   integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz in the Bessel norms. Approximation of that
   769	  108|   function in $L^1$ by compact smooth functions, followed by integration by
   770	  109|   parts for the approximants, proves $\langle\tau_yz,w\rangle_E \to 0$ as $|y|
   771	  110|   \to \infty$. Thus, $\tau_yz$ tends weakly to zero. For compact $K$,
   772	  111|   $\|K\tau_yz\| \to 0$: otherwise compactness supplies a norm-convergent
   773	  112|   subsequence with nonzero norm, while bounded linear testing makes its limit
   774	  113|   zero. For unit $z$ it follows that
   775	  114|   \[
   776	  115|     \|S_E(h)+K\|
   777	  116|     \ge\liminf_{|y|\to\infty}\|(S_E(h)+K)\tau_yz\|
   778	  117|     \ge\|S_E(h)z\|.
   779	  118|   \]
   780	  119|   Taking the supremum over $z$ gives $\|S_E(h)+K\| \ge \|S_E(h)\|$. The
   781	  120|   isometric velocity reversal $\mathcal{R}(u,v) = (u,-v)$ satisfies $S_E(-h) =
   782	  121|   \mathcal{R} S_E(h)\mathcal{R}$ by the full free Fourier matrix. The group law
   783	  122|   yields $1 \le \|S_E(-h)\|\|S_E(h)\| = \|S_E(h)\|^2$. This
   784	  123|   proves~\eqref{E:symplectic-compact-young-baseline}.
   785	  124| 
   786	  125|   Finally, $P_j-S_E(\ell_j)$ is compact. Telescoping the finite ordered product
   787	  126|   against its free product gives a finite sum of bounded--compact--bounded
   788	  127|   products, hence a compact difference. Only the free factors are combined by
   789	  128|   the group law; no noisy factors are commuted. The same translation argument
   790	  129|   proves \eqref{E:symplectic-compact-product-baseline}. A zero length gives $P_j
   791	  130|   = I$. All assertions are at fixed finite horizons and products; no uniform
   792	  131|   compact approximation in a radius, horizon or number of factors is asserted.
   793	  132|   This proves Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free}.
   794	  133| \end{proof}

   797	  205| \begin{theorem}[The computed occupation ceiling]\label{T:intrinsic-occupation-ceiling}
   798	  206|   For every variational value over nonnegative controls coefficient
   799	  207|   $\mathfrak{c}$,
   800	  208|   \begin{align}
   801	  209|     S_{\mathfrak{c}}^{\mathrm{pos}}
   802	  210|     &\le U_{\mathfrak{c}}
   803	  211|     :=\mathfrak{c}^m k
   804	  212|     \left[\frac{\alpha^{\alpha/2}C_{\rm occ}}{8q^{q/2}}\right]^{1/k}
   805	  213|     \label{E:occupation-score-ceiling}\\
   806	  214|     &=\mathfrak{c}^m(2\zeta)^{\alpha/(2k)}
   807	  215|     F_0(\mathcal{E}_\zeta^{\mathcal{O}}),\qquad \zeta>0.\notag
   808	  216|   \end{align}
   809	  217|   In particular, the original moment constant satisfies $C_2(\Gamma,a) \le U_2$
   810	  218|   for every original model. This ceiling is not asserted to be attained or equal
   811	  219|   to $C_2$.
   812	  220| \end{theorem}
   813	  221| 
   814	  222| \begin{proof}
   815	  223|   Fix $\Psi$ and write $v = v_\Psi$, $C = C_{\rm occ}$ and $\beta = \alpha/4$.
   816	  224|   Lemma~\ref{L:occupation-rayleigh-selection} gives $I_\Psi^2 \le
   817	  225|   \sqrt{vC}T^\beta-T+\varepsilon$ for some $T > 0$. Bound it by the supremum
   818	  226|   over all $T \ge 0$ before sending $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. If $v = 0$, that
   819	  227|   supremum is zero. If $v > 0$, the derivative $\beta\sqrt{vC}T^{\beta-1}-1$
   820	  228|   strictly decreases from infinity to $-1$. Its unique positive zero is $T_* =
   821	  229|   (\beta\sqrt{vC})^{1/(1-\beta)}$. The global maximum equals
   822	  230|   $(q/4)(\alpha/4)^{\alpha/q}(vC)^{2/q}$. In both cases,
   823	  231|   \[
   824	  232|     I_\Psi\le Dv^{1/q},\qquad
   825	  233|     D=\sqrt{q/4}(\alpha/4)^{\alpha/(2q)}C^{1/q}.
   826	  234|   \]
   827	  235|   The scalar function $\mathfrak{c} Dv^{1/q}-v/2$ vanishes at zero, tends to
   828	  236|   minus infinity, and has strictly decreasing derivative. Its unique positive
   829	  237|   maximum is at $v_* = (2\mathfrak{c} D/q)^{q/k}$, with value $kv_*/2$. Direct
   830	  238|   positive-power algebra gives
   831	  239|   \[
   832	  240|     (2D/q)^q=q^{-q/2}(\alpha/4)^{\alpha/2}C .
   833	  241|   \]
   834	  242|   Since $k+\alpha = 3$, the maximum is precisely $U_{\mathfrak{c}}$
   835	  243|   in~\eqref{E:occupation-score-ceiling}, with denominator eight. Substitution
   836	  244|   of~\eqref{E:raw-occupation-ratio} gives the second form, retaining the factor
   837	  245|   $(2\zeta)^{\alpha/(2k)}$. Take the supremum over the smooth positive-control
   838	  246|   class. Theorem~\ref{T:intrinsic-second-moment} identifies $C_2 =
   839	  247|   S_2^{\mathrm{pos}}$, proving the moment ceiling. The penalty factor cancels
   840	  248|   its energy scaling, so the ceiling is independent of $\zeta$. This proves
   841	  249|   Theorem~\ref{T:intrinsic-occupation-ceiling}.
   842	  250| \end{proof}

   546	`damped_homogeneous_norms_full_paper` with `G := waveGreen d`. -/
   547	theorem damped_homogeneous_norms_full_wave {alpha alpha0 : ℝ} {Γ μ : Measure (Rd d)}

   551	        Integrable (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.exp (-(θ * (p.1 + p.2))) * |p.1 - p.2| ^ (-alpha0) *
   552	          ∫ ξ, waveHat p.1 ξ * waveHat p.2 ξ ∂μ) P2 ∧
   553	        Integrable (fun l : ℝ => l ^ (alpha0 - 1) * resolvent μ (θ + l)) L0) ∧
   554	      0 ≤ N2sq alpha0 θ μ ∧
   555	      IntegrableOn (fun s => Real.exp (-(θ * s)) * (waveGreen d s univ).toReal) (Ioi 0) ∧

   558	      N2sq alpha0 θ μ = θ ^ (-(4 - alpha - alpha0)) * N2sq alpha0 1 μ) ∧
   559	    (∀ M : ℝ, Integrable (N2onIntegrand (d := d) alpha0 1 (Ioi M)) (P2.prod μ) ∧
   560	      Integrable (N2onOuter alpha0 1 (Ioi M) μ) P2 ∧ 0 ≤ N2tailSq alpha0 M μ) ∧
   561	    Tendsto (fun M => N1tail alpha0 M μ) atTop (𝓝 0) ∧
   562	    Tendsto (fun M => N2tailSq alpha0 M μ) atTop (𝓝 0) ∧
   563	    Tendsto (fun M => N2tail alpha0 M μ) atTop (𝓝 0) ∧
   564	    (∀ θ : ℝ, 0 < θ → ∀ g : Rd d → ℝ≥0, IsMultiplier g →

   568	        N1on alpha0 θ S (smoothed μ g) ≤ N1on alpha0 θ S' μ ∧
   569	        Integrable (N2onOuter alpha0 θ S (smoothed μ g)) P2 ∧
   570	        Integrable (N2onOuter alpha0 θ S' μ) P2 ∧
   571	        0 ≤ N2onSq alpha0 θ S (smoothed μ g) ∧
   572	        N2onSq alpha0 θ S (smoothed μ g) ≤ N2onSq alpha0 θ S' μ) ∧
   573	    (∀ η : ℝ, 0 ≤ η → IsMultiplier (gaussMult (d := d) η)) ∧
   574	    (∀ g g' : Rd d → ℝ≥0, IsMultiplier g → IsMultiplier g' → IsMultiplier (g * g')) ∧
   575	    (∀ v : ℝ, 0 ≤ v →
   576	      GreenMass (fun s => gaussKernel v ∗ waveGreen d s) ∧
   577	      (∀ θ : ℝ, 0 < θ →
   578	        IntegrableOn (fun s => Real.exp (-(θ * s)) *
   579	          ((gaussKernel v ∗ waveGreen d s) univ).toReal) (Ioi 0) ∧

   581	        N0 (fun s => gaussKernel v ∗ waveGreen d s) θ = θ ^ (-(2 : ℝ))) ∧
   582	      (∀ θ : ℝ, ∀ S : Set ℝ,
   583	        N2GreenSq alpha0 θ S μ (fun s => gaussKernel v ∗ waveGreen d s) =

   148	def gammaEps (Γ : Measure (Rd d)) (ε : ℝ) (x : Rd d) : ℝ :=

    19	With the continuous extension of `α π/(2 sin(π α/2))` at `α = 0`, which is `1`,
    20	`R_0 = 1` and the `R_α` form holds at the witness (`1 ≤ 2`).

    24	import StratonovichHAMSecondMoment.SpectralMassIdentity

    33	/-- Lebesgue measure on `ℝ¹` has spectral measure `δ_0`. -/
    34	theorem leb_spectral : IsSpectralMeasure (volume : Measure (Rd 1)) (Measure.dirac 0) := by
    35	  intro φ
    36	  rw [integral_dirac]
    37	  simp
    38	
    39	theorem dirac_homog : SpectralHomog.SpectralHomogeneous (Measure.dirac (0 : Rd 1)) 0 := by
    40	  intro A _ c hc
    41	  rw [Real.rpow_zero, ENNReal.ofReal_one, one_mul, Measure.dirac_apply, Measure.dirac_apply]
    42	  by_cases h0 : (0 : Rd 1) ∈ A
    43	  · rw [Set.indicator_of_mem h0, Set.indicator_of_mem ((Set.zero_mem_smul_set_iff hc.ne').2 h0)]
    44	  · rw [Set.indicator_of_notMem h0,
    45	      Set.indicator_of_notMem (fun h => h0 ((Set.zero_mem_smul_set_iff hc.ne').1 h))]

    47	/-- `A_sp(g) = 1` for Lebesgue `Γ` and every real unit test `g` on `ℝ¹`. -/
    48	theorem energy_leb {g : Rd 1 → ℝ} (hg : IsUnitTest g) : spatialEnergy volume g = 1 := by
    49	  have hQc : Continuous (fun x => g x ^ 2) := hg.1.continuous.pow 2
    50	  have hQs : HasCompactSupport (fun x => g x ^ 2) :=
    51	    hg.2.1.comp_left (g := fun r : ℝ => r ^ 2) (by norm_num)
    52	  have h := (SpatialSmoothRatio.integral_conv_mul volume hQc hQs hQc hQs).2
    53	  have hconv : ∀ x, VariationalDilation.conv volume (fun x => g x ^ 2) x = 1 := by
    54	    intro x
    55	    rw [VariationalDilation.conv, integral_sub_left_eq_self (fun y => g y ^ 2) volume x]
    56	    exact hg.2.2
    57	  simp_rw [hconv, one_mul] at h
    58	  rw [spatialEnergy, ← h, hg.2.2]

    61	theorem fourier_bound_alpha_zero_refuted :
    62	    ¬ (∀ (Γ μ : Measure (Rd 1)) [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure Γ] [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ],
    63	        IsSpectralMeasure Γ μ → ∀ alpha : ℝ, SpectralHomog.SpectralHomogeneous μ alpha →
    64	        alpha < 2 → ∀ g : Rd 1 → ℝ, IsUnitTest g →
    65	        spatialEnergy Γ g ≤
    66	          2 ^ (1 + alpha) * SpectralMassIdentity.ralpha μ alpha * gradEnergy g ^ (alpha / 2)) := by
    67	  intro h
    68	  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := SpatialSmoothRatio.exists_unitTest 1
    69	  have h1 := h volume (Measure.dirac 0) leb_spectral 0 dirac_homog (by norm_num) g hg

    71	  norm_num [SpectralMassIdentity.ralpha] at h1

    76	      SpectralHomog.resolvent (Measure.dirac (0 : Rd 1)) 1 * gradEnergy g ^ ((0 : ℝ) / 2) :=

    78	    (gradEnergy_pos one_pos hg)).2.2.2.2.2

2257	## FiniteWick (whole result)
  2258	
  2259	A reusable foundation with no manuscript label of its own, proved in full with
  2260	nothing supplied. It formalizes the Wick (Isserlis) step in the proof of
  2261	`L:terminal-wick` (`notes/notes_stratonovich_ham_second_moment.tex` at
  2262	`a284420`): the formula `E:terminal-wick-formula` (lines 3619-3622) with "each
  2263	pairing has coefficient one" and "if `m+n` is odd, the expectation is zero"
  2264	(line 3638), the Gaussian moment computation of the proof (lines 3662-3675), the
  2265	moment bound of lines 3651-3656, and the pointwise positivity and comparison of
  2266	covariance products (lines 3693-3695). The chain integrals themselves are in
  2267	`TerminalWick`. Abstractions: a pairing (pair partition) of a finite set `S` of a
  2268	linearly ordered finite type is a fixed-point-free involution of `S`, normalized
  2269	to the identity off `S` so that each pair partition is exactly one function
  2270	(`pairings`); its weight takes one factor `c(a, p a)` per pair, at the smaller
  2271	element `a < p a`, so every unordered pair contributes once with coefficient one
  2272	(`pairWeight`); `wickSum c S` is the sum of the weights. For `S` all of
  2273	`Fin (2k)` these are the pair partitions `Pi_k` of the TeX. The double factorial
  2274	is `Nat.doubleFactorial` with natural subtraction, so `(2*0-1)!! = 0!! = 1`, the
  2275	empty-product convention of line 3639. Gaussian side: `stdPi N` (from
  2276	`GaussianIBP`) is the law of `N` independent standard Gaussians, and Mathlib
  2277	defines `multivariateGaussian 0 K` as the image of the standard Gaussian under
  2278	`x -> sqrt(K) x` (`CFC.sqrt`). `CenteredGaussianField W K P` states the TeX's
  2279	hypothesis "centered real Gaussian field with covariance `K`" (lines 3601-3602)
  2280	as: for every finite family of points `p : Fin n -> X`, the matrix
  2281	`(K(p_a, p_b))` is positive semidefinite and `(W(p_a))_a` has law
  2282	`multivariateGaussian 0 (K(p_a, p_b))`. Implicit hypotheses made explicit:
  2283	`K` positive semidefinite (otherwise Mathlib's `multivariateGaussian 0 K` is the
  2284	Dirac mass at `0`), and every integral identity for Gaussian monomials (products
  2285	of finitely many coordinates or field values) comes with the integrability of
  2286	its integrand, either as a conjunct or in a separate theorem. The exception is the bridge
  2287	`integral_multivariateGaussian_eq` for an arbitrary continuous `F`: it is an
  2288	equality of Lean's totalized integrals and assumes no integrability, so for a
  2289	non-integrable `F` (for instance `exp(x_0^4)` under a nondegenerate Gaussian)
  2290	both sides are the junk value `0`; integrability transfers only through the
  2291	separate equivalence `integrable_multivariateGaussian_iff`. No hypothesis is carried unused. Proof-route
  2292	differences: the Gaussian identity is proved by Stein's recursion
  2293	`E[g_e F(g)] = E[partial_e F(g)]` (`GaussianIBP.integral_coord_mul_eq_of_growth`)
  2294	for `x = A g`, expanded along the partner of the least index
  2295	(`wickSum_eq_sum_erase`), instead of differentiating the moment generating
  2296	function (lines 3664-3673); the conclusion is the same. The moment bound
  2297	`E(prod_{a<n} W(p_a))^2 <= (2n-1)!! V^n` (`CenteredGaussianField.sq_moment_le`)
  2298	is the Wick formula for the `2n` values together with the count of `(2k-1)!!`
  2299	pairings (`card_pairings_even`, `wickSum_abs_le`) and `|K(x,y)| <= V`
  2300	(`CenteredGaussianField.abs_le`), instead of Hoelder's inequality and `L^(2n)`
  2301	Gaussian moments; the bound is the same. No conclusion is narrower than the
  2302	TeX step it formalizes. Junk values: `wickSum` is a finite sum, and every Bochner
  2303	integral of a Gaussian monomial appears with a proof of integrability; only the
  2304	continuous-`F` bridge above can equate two junk values, and the monomial
  2305	results apply it to integrable monomials. Refutations
  2306	(`refutations/finite-wick/`), all combinatorial or one-dimensional controls
  2307	without junk-value reliance: `PairingCount` (`(2k)!/k!` pairings of a `2k`-set;
  2308	`k = 2` gives `12`, not `3`), `AbsBound` (the pairing-sum bound without
  2309	`(2k-1)!!`; `c = 1` on `Fin 4`), `NonnegDropped` (pairing sums nonnegative for
  2310	arbitrary real weights, not a covariance; `c = -1` on `Fin 2`) and
  2311	`FourthMoment` (`E x^4 = 1` for a standard Gaussian `x`, an actual Gaussian
  2312	law; the Wick formula gives `3`). Not
  2313	formalized here: everything about the chain measures, the `L^2`-valued integrals
  2314	and the series (see `TerminalWick`). The four route definitions `unpair`,
  2315	`pairUp`, `matBound` and `monoDeriv` are public but are not listed as claims;
  2316	they appear only inside the statements of the auxiliary rows below.

  4723	  ball-mass formula. Since $\mu$ is Radon, $V < \infty$, and continuity from
  4724	  above gives $\mu(\{0\}) = \lim_{R\downarrow0}VR^\alpha = 0$. By the layer-cake
  4725	  identity and Tonelli's theorem,
  4726	  \[

  4728	    =\int_0^h\mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le u^{-1}\})\ud u
  4729	    =V\int_0^h u^{-\alpha}\ud u.

  4732	  $\alpha < 1$, the last expression is the finite quantity
  4733	  in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-radial}. This computation uses ball masses, not a radial

    30	\begin{lemma}[Free wave form and compact Young baseline]
    31	  \label{L:symplectic-free}
    32	  There is a bounded isometric skew-adjoint $J_E$ on $E$, with $J_E^2 = -I$,
    33	  such that
    34	  \[
    35	    \omega(z,w)=\langle z,J_Ew\rangle_E
    36	    =\langle u,g\rangle_{H^{1/2},H^{-1/2}}
    37	    -\langle f,v\rangle_{H^{1/2},H^{-1/2}},
    38	    \quad z=(u,v),\quad w=(f,g).
    39	  \]
    40	  The free group preserves $\omega$. For bounded real smooth $b$, the force
    41	  $B(b)(u,v) = (0,bu)$ obeys $\omega(B(b)z,w)+\omega(z,B(b)w) = 0$.
    42	
    43	  Let $1/2 < \theta < 1$ and let $X \in C^\theta([0,T];\mathcal{K}(E))$ start at
    44	  zero, with $U_X$ its left Young evolution. Then
    45	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-compact-young-baseline}
    46	    U_X(t,s)-I\in\mathcal{K}(E),\qquad
    47	    \|S_E(t)U_X(t,s)S_E(-s)\|
    48	    \ge\|S_E(t-s)\|\ge1,\qquad 0\le s\le t\le T .
    49	  \end{equation}
    50	  More generally, for finitely many such paths $X_j$ starting at zero on $[0,B]$
    51	  and lengths $0 \le \ell_j \le B$, put $P_j = S_E(\ell_j)U_{X_j}(\ell_j,0)$.
    52	  Then
    53	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-compact-product-baseline}
    54	    P_N\cdots P_0-S_E\Big(\sum_{j=0}^N\ell_j\Big)\in\mathcal{K}(E),
    55	    \qquad
    56	    \|P_N\cdots P_0\|
    57	    \ge\left\|S_E\Big(\sum_{j=0}^N\ell_j\Big)\right\|\ge1 .
    58	  \end{equation}
    59	  These norm bounds require neither Gaussian nor Hamiltonian operator paths.
    60	\end{lemma}

    64	  onto real isometry to $L^2\times L^2$. Define $J_{\rm symp}(q,p) = (p,-q)$ and
    65	  $J_E = C_{\rm bal}^{-1}J_{\rm symp}C_{\rm bal}$. This gives all stated
    66	  operator properties and $J_E(f,g) = (\Lambda^{-1}g,-\Lambda f)$. The two
    67	  displayed dualities follow from the balanced $L^2$ pairing. No $L^2$ pairing

    69	
    70	  In balanced Fourier coordinates, the free matrix is
    71	  \[
    72	    W_t(\xi)=
    73	    \begin{pmatrix}
    74	      \cos(tk)&\langle\xi\rangle\sin(tk)/k\\
    75	      -k\sin(tk)/\langle\xi\rangle&\cos(tk)
    76	    \end{pmatrix},\qquad k=|\xi|.
    77	  \]
    78	  At zero it is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, by
    79	  the continuous sine quotient. Direct matrix multiplication gives
    80	  $W_t^{\mathsf{T}}J_{\rm symp}W_t = J_{\rm symp}$, since its determinant is
    81	  $\cos^2(tk)+\sin^2(tk) = 1$, also at zero. The entries are real, even and
    82	  bounded on finite time horizons. Integrating the identity against real-phase
    83	  Fourier vectors with Hermitian symmetry is legitimate by $L^2$
    84	  Cauchy--Schwarz. It gives $\omega(S_E(t)z,S_E(t)w) = \omega(z,w)$ on all $E$.
    85	  Equivalently one may first use Schwartz phases and then density. No rough
    86	  generator derivative or frequency-zero trace is used.
    87	
    88	  Finally, $\|bu\|_{H^{-1/2}} \le \|bu\|_2 \le \|b\|_\infty\|u\|_{H^{1/2}}$.
    89	  Duality for these $L^2$ functions gives the absolutely integrable cancellation
    90	  $-\int fbu+\int ubf = 0$. This is skewness for $\omega$, not for the $E$
    91	  Hilbert inner product. The Young construction of
    92	  Proposition~\ref{P:constant-young-linear} applies on $\mathcal{L}(E)$: its
    93	  proof uses completeness and operator multiplication of norm one, exactly as on

    96	    \sum_j\big(X(t_{j+1})-X(t_j)\big)U_X(t_j,s)
    97	  \]

    99	  of the compact ideal gives the first assertion
   100	  in~\eqref{E:symplectic-compact-young-baseline}. Bounded composition then shows
   101	  that the physical endpoint differs from $S_E(t-s)$ by a compact operator.

   103	  We prove the required compact-perturbation bound for this whole-space phase.

   107	  integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz in the Bessel norms. Approximation of that

   127	  products, hence a compact difference. Only the free factors are combined by

   130	  = I$. All assertions are at fixed finite horizons and products; no uniform
   131	  compact approximation in a radius, horizon or number of factors is asserted.
   132	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free}.
   133	\end{proof}

  2531	\begin{lemma}[Exact cutoffs for finite Gaussian words]\label{L:finite-word-cutoff}
  2532	  Let $g_{ij}$, $1 \le i \le M$, $1 \le j \le m_i$, be independent standard real
  2533	  Gaussian coordinates, grouped by color $i$, and let $\mathscr{X}$ be a complex
  2534	  Hilbert space. On Gaussian polynomials with coefficients in $\mathscr{X}$ set
  2535	  \[
  2536	    J_i=\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}M_{g_{ij}}\otimes K_{ij},
  2537	  \]
  2538	  where each $K_{ij}$ is bounded on $\mathscr{X}$. Let $F_0,\ldots,F_n$ be
  2539	  bounded operators acting only on $\mathscr{X}$. Fix a word $i_1,\ldots,i_n$,
  2540	  and let $r_i$ be the number of its occurrences of color $i$. If $N_i \ge r_i$
  2541	  and $P$ projects each color onto total Hermite degree at most $N_i$, then, for
  2542	  every $v \in \mathscr{X}$,
  2543	  \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-word-cutoff}
  2544	    \begin{split}
  2545	      &(I\otimes F_n)(PJ_{i_n}P)(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
  2546	      (PJ_{i_1}P)(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v)\\
  2547	      &\qquad=(I\otimes F_n)J_{i_n}(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
  2548	      J_{i_1}(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v).
  2549	    \end{split}
  2550	  \end{equation}
  2551	  The equality holds for finite sums and for Bochner integrals of such words
  2552	  whenever the displayed vector integrals exist.
  2553	\end{lemma}
  2554	
  2555	\begin{proof}
  2556	  In normalized Hermite coordinates, multiplication by $g_{ij}$ maps
  2557	  $h_{\boldsymbol a}$ to $\sqrt{a_{ij}+1}\,h_{\boldsymbol a+e_{ij}}
  2558	  +\sqrt{a_{ij}}\,h_{\boldsymbol a-e_{ij}}$; the second term is zero if $a_{ij}
  2559	  = 0$. Thus, it changes the total degree of color $i$ by one and leaves all
  2560	  other color degrees unchanged. The operators $I\otimes F_l$ leave every
  2561	  Gaussian degree unchanged. After the first $l$ insertions, the uncompressed
  2562	  word therefore has color-$i$ degree at most $r_i(l) = |\{j\le l:i_j=i\}| \le
  2563	  r_i \le N_i$. This is an induction starting from degree zero in every color.
  2564	  Consequently, $P$ is the identity both before and after every insertion along
  2565	  that word. Induction on $l$ now proves \eqref{E:finite-word-cutoff}. The
  2566	  lowering term has been retained: the assertion includes creation followed by
  2567	  annihilation and all resulting self-contractions. Linearity and equality of
  2568	  the vector integrands prove the last assertion. This is an equality of
  2569	  selected finite words, not of full propagators at a fixed cutoff. This proves
  2570	  Lemma~\ref{L:finite-word-cutoff}.
  2571	\end{proof}
